item.title: Re: "The Man of Nobody"
item.content:encoded:
Summoned via PM:

Hi there Identity8866. Let’s take a look at your concept.

Overall, the concept was interesting at first, especially since you seem to be questioning the nature of human interactions and whether truly “No man is an island”.

Unfortunately, the concept falls apart rapidly due to plot inconsistencies or overcomplications that are not well explained. Why, for example, do people do when this happens? I believe it’s never explained / hinted at throughout your concept. Who placed this curse on him, and why?

Secondly, I don’t understand the nature of the anomaly. Okay, so they die “horrific” deaths, but how and why in those manners? You realise that a “horrific” death can be incredibly subjective, right? Some people would be terrified of dying alone, for example. More importantly, is there a reason why they die in such a manner?

Additionally, the concept itself is vague as “relationship” can mean pretty much anything? You mention “friend”, “enemy” and “loved one”, but isn’t an acquaintance also considered a relationship? Wouldn’t the Foundation agents who try and contain the man also be affected then?

Finally, I don’t understand that whole angle with suicide patients. How are they being “helped”?

Overall, there are too many plot issues for me to understand this fully. If you do decide to revise the concept / respond below, do drop me another PM and I’ll take another look. Best of luck!

item.title: Re: (Seeking Greenlight) the Survivors
item.content:encoded:
Summoned via PM:

Hi there EnderDragon101. Let’s take a look at your concept.

Overall, I agree with Quadraginta’s assessment: the concept sounds too ambitious, with you including multiple anomalies with little to no explanation as to their purpose or intention.

Mind you, it’s not about whether the concept is heavily sci-fi or not. It’s what you do with the many elements you’ve cited. What does the GOC have to do shooting down an alien ship, for example? What does “Galactic.Co” have to do with the alien’s purpose for being on earth? Why cross a human with an orca to make the alien? Is it just to make them look/sound cool? Finally, the whole description of SCP-xxxx-2 and SCP-xxxx-3 is overly confusing. It’s not clear why you needed to have two different materials in the first place, and what their significance is to the Foundation or the GOC.

The danger of picking a sci-fi setting is most beginning authors feel that they can get away with including multiple out-of-this-world / bizarre concepts and then make the excuse that “Oh, it’s just because it’s sci-fi” for their existence. Sorry, but the base rules of storytelling still apply: tell us what’s happening in your Central Narrative segment, and ensure that all the elements are clearly linked together. A majority of your Central Narrative atm is simply describing the SCP, and not going into enough detail about the actual narrative.

I hope you continue working on the concept though. The strength of a sci-fi concept is that you can really think out of the box, but some restraint is needed here. If you decide to revise the concept / respond below, do drop me another PM and I’ll take another look. Best of luck!

item.title: Good intentions
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: Yes

Page Type: SCP Article

Elevator Pitch: A semi-sentient liquid metal that bonds with a persons nervous system and tries to protect that person from harm, but ultimately does more harm than good.

Central Narrative: The SCP is an unknown liquid metal that enters a persons body through the skin, bonding with that persons nervous system. Whenever an object/person comes into contact with the skin of the host, the metal will rush through the persons nerves to the point of impact, surfacing out of the skin to form a shield that protects the person from physical trauma. The SCP accidentally damages the nerves when it travels through them, causing intense pain in the host in the short run, and loss of fine motor skills to loss of all feelings in limbs in the long run. Even if the SCP is inactive in the host, over time the host will develop symptoms similar to long-term mercury poisoning, which will result in death after 10-15 months.

+ show
- hide

The SCP will only have one host at a time, and will not transfer to another while the previous host still lives. It initially transfers by skin to skin contact with the previous hosts corpse, however if the SCP is without a host for an extended period of time, it will leave the previous hosts body and seek out the nearest human to bond with. If it is unable to find a host after leaving the previous host, it will become increasingly aggressive and stronger to break out and locate a new host.

Due to the SCP reacting to even the smallest contacts with the skin, it becomes nigh impossible for the host to complete small tasks, and even a small shift in their clothing can set of the SCP. Monitoring the effects the SCP has on its hosts is extremely difficult, because the SCP prevents the foundation from taking any samples while the host still lives, and most forms of scans are ineffective.

In order to contain the anomaly, the foundation will expose a D-class in a medically induced coma to the SCP, and try to keep them alive for as long as possible. After the death of the D-class, a new D-class will be put into a coma before transferring the SCP to them.


Hook/Attention-Grabber: Something created to protect humans ends up damaging them in the long run.

Additional Notes: Linked to the broken god.

item.title: Re: A Photo Book of Murderers
item.content:encoded:
[+] Open for crit
– hide block

There is an eighty percent chance that within the first hour if the person whose photo is removed their personality will stop being overwritten however for every hour it decreases by twenty percent. And for every hour less and less of the subject's sanity is retained.

This feels … really video game-y? Like just the way it works makes it feel like it's a cursed item from a game and not like, a thing which exists? I think because of the like…rigid, one size fits all progression which feels like it's kinda glossing over how everyone reacts to stuff differently and so it'd affect different people to different intensities and with different recovery times.

Beyond this, my core issue with this idea is that at it's core, it's "thing what turns you insane", which is, generally not very interesting to me. The angle of tying this into the brutality of asylums isn't a bad idea here but it feels underutilised: it feels, almost more like something your pointing at to say 'wow isn't this horrifying' than like, something actually in the story that you're grappling with and showing the horror of?

It also feels like it doesn't go anywhere: there's no real arc or growth through this, so like, you might highlight the malpractice but you're not really telling a story with it so much as showing some material that is shocking? And it feels like this needs e.g. a single character or something progressing through this that builds up to some kinda ending that grants closure?

I don't think this idea is dead in the water so much as it feels like it needs to take all the pieces you've assembled so far and then use them to do something, y'know?

item.title: Re: The Petrifying Statue
item.content:encoded:
Hello, let me make some questions and suggestions here, bear in mind I am not an official critter, though :)

First of all I know it hurts to hear this but this is basically reverse SCP-173. It is a statue and it kills people in horrible fashion triggered by them looking at it. It isn't a bad idea per se but it feels very Series I and currently these kind of stories are not very popular so I think even if you made it into the main page you would get downvoted pretty hard.

Secondly, there is no narrative here, you are just explaining what the anomaly is. What is the arc, who are the characters, what is the purpose? Why should I care about this article and what should I feel and think of it?

Your idea has terrifying implications: what if the statues around us in parks and public spaces were petrified people? If so, are they conscious? Is it possible to revert this state? I think this is a concept you should explore.

Also, from personal experience, writing AWCY is harder than it seems. Not every art anomaly must be tied to them so if you want to pursue this aspect you should flesh it out, give it a clear purpose, explore the anartist's intentions and what message they are trying to pass. Make this a plot twist or turn of events instead of just a tag to your story: what if the petrified people were volunteer artists who wanted to become art themselves? What if the petrified statue is the anartist themself?

Lots of what ifs to explore and figure out but by the end of it you'll have a much more fleshed out article that will have a bigger chance to make it into the official list. Good luck!


Forum category: Writing Help / Help: Ideas Critique
Forum thread: The Petrifying Statue

item.title: Re: (Still) Awaiting Greenlight / The Book of the Sinners
item.content:encoded:
[+] Open for crit
– hide block

If no human voluntarily tests themselves within a day, the book will choose a sinful challenger within a certain radius around it.

This is generally a bad idea: forcing someone to use a scp is generally a lot less impactful than exploring what happens when someone chooses to use it.

Each of the two will give a unique perspective about the realm of the sins, the sins themselves (so to say their representatives), the seven tests, and the ones who failed the trial.

This feels like the meat of the article and my biggest issue is that I still don't have a good idea of what this is going to be like. Or, rather, my concern is that it feels very passive: there's no like, driving force here where we're invested in the outcome of this because there's no stakes to it? It doesn't really matter to use whether they succeed or not because it doesn't really change much. It could work without stakes if the actual tests are interesting, or with good characterisation of the researchers and like, a big emotional arc where they really grow over the course of the testing, but I'm not really sure what your plans are in regard to that?

You mention there's a prize if someone passes all the tests: this could be the thing that provides stakes but like, it really depends on what it is? If it's big enough, the Foundation might feel justified in throwing some d-class at this to try to get the prize, and that might get around the first issue I raised.

item.title: SCP Idea: The Earworm
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlight: Yes
Page Type: SCP article
Genre: Horror
Page Layout: Basic, Containment Procedures, Description of SCPs effects, than 2 interview logs and an incident report detailing a mass outbreak of the SCP.
Elevator Pitch: An human infecting parasite that is activated by song.

The Earworm is a keter class entity due to it being a small difficult to spot, wide spread parasitic entity capable of emitting a cognitohazardous noise.

Earworms will hang in bushes and form cacoons in the shape of small music notes, at which point they will begin produce a song.

The Earworm's song compels those who hear it to eat it, at which point, the stomach acids will dissolve the cacoon and Earworm will burrow out of the stomach and make it's way to the brain, burrowing into the left side of the cerebrum then inject an amnestic so the host forgets eating the cacoon. It will remain there in a hibernating state until the host hears music.

+ show block
– hide block

Once the host hears music, the Earworm will awaken and begin eating the hosts Cerebellum, growing in size and connecting to the Host's nervous system. During this process the host will be unable to get the song that activated the earworm out of their head.

Over time, the Earworm will eat and replace more and more of the hosts brain, eventually removing the ability for complex thought and turning the host into a feral creature incapable of speaking in anything other than the song. At this point the Earworm, now resembling brain tissue itself, will lay eggs in the remains of the hosts brain and the host will be drawn to populated yet rural areas. Once the eggs hatch the Earworm larvae will eat the rest of the hosts brain and burrow out to find a place where they can make a cacoon.

This leaves the host completely under control of the now adult Earworm, which has completely replaced the hosts brain.

Hook: The idea is to start of with a relatable experience (A song being so stuck in your head) and make you question yourself every time you experience it.

item.title: Re: Thaumiel Factory Failure (seeking greenlight)
item.content:encoded:
Thank you for taking a look at my concept yet again.

+ show block
– hide block

My answers:

how would they know what Thaumiel class is?

They don't. They simply try to manufacture Objects that could aid the foundation, who would then in turn be classified as Thaumiel.

Why would they assume Foundation personnel would trust their products

This is the reason this individual does not speak to the foundation at all while building the factory. They want the products to speak for themselves.

let alone pay for them?

Since this concept would have been to long if I included details about the individual i left them out. This individual inherits a vast amount of money from their dead family members. This money will be used to set everything necessary up. They have a genuine good heart and witnesses the foundation helping humans against an anomaly. Since he is not directly from the foundation he does not know of the inner workings and events, i.e. he thinks that the foundation in its entirety is completely good and would never do anything evil.
With that in mind, he tries to fabricate objects that would help them while also receiving money in return for his work. He doesn't even think about the foundation ceasing his property. Since his family is quite rich he has always been taught that money is his highest priority and he follows those teachings.

It's already a stretch of disbelief for me to believe that the Foundation just happened to not notice this person witnessing a containment incident

That makes sense, but I also find it hard to believe that the foundation catches every single person that witnesses a containment incident. Someone will slip by somehow eventually but this time it's a nice person.

and said person just happens to have the factory means to produce anomalies somehow

This Person does not happen to have it. He builds it himself. How he does that is something I am still working on. Plan is currently that he uses his money to hire people that know a thing or two and compiles their knowledge.

When you add in the fact that they somehow learned enough about the Foundation to figure out the kind of anomalies that would be considered useful

I have thought about that part. Since he himself would be confronted with anomalies or at least some knowledge of them he would know some dangers, like looking at them or directly touching them. He is building a abnormal factory after all. So the stuff he would produce are things he thinks are useful like gloves that make your hands indestructable, boxes that lock things inside with no way of opening them from the inside, glasses that protect your mind from seeing things and hazmat suits to keep nasty stuff away.

Since this individual has knowledge on how to construct a factory and knowledge of the abnormal, I dont think this is too far fetched. Also he has no direct contact to the foundation. That is the reason he programs a virus that randomly infects printers etc. to print that messages because he knows the foundation will pick up the signal and find him. He has not done so sooner because he wanted his products to be finished before contacting them.

Why do you want the factory to be the work of one person?

I want the factory to have 1 important person in charge, who hired other people to help him build it, yet him pulling all the strings.

Why do you want them to just randomly and conveniently find out a lot of information about the Foundation, thereby making the Foundation look incompetent in terms of information security?

I dont want to do that. I want 1 single mistake from the foundation and 1 single rich person with a good heart and a too naive way of thinking to clash and culminate into this story.

their scheme is disturbed by something as mundane as a coal company

The coal company part is definetely something that could get changed, but I don't think it is huge problem. The individual needs money to build up his little factory and the coal company makes prices go up by buying all needed materials in the area, thereby making it more expensive for him to buy said materials. Also, he still is a good person that abides by the rules and just ignores it. His money eventually runs low and he begins to sell businesses that his family own that gave him money in the first place in order to fullfill his current dream. He risks it all and gets nothing because he is too naive and simple minded.

How open are you to changing these elements to make the story more believable and the main character more of a relatable individual and not an excessively exceptional caricature?

I am open to any changes that make the story better/clearer without completely changing its direction.

I feel like so far you've set a lot of difficult challenges up for the story

I want this story to work and am willing to put in as much effort as needed by me. That being said, I really should make a draft before saying that.

Thank you so much for all your input. As i said before, even though this entire conversation might not lead to a greenlight by you, I am still very grateful for the time and thought you have given me.
Thanks again!

item.title: Re: Getting Sandbox Feedback without Greenlight?
item.content:encoded:
Agreeing with Hexick's post above, and noting that if you're looking to work on your writing skills specific to SCP articles, you don't necessarily need to ask for feedback on a whole draft. If you're seeking to improve clinical tone, for example, you can post short excerpts in the Questions Desk forum to ask for opinions on what to improve. You can also ask for tips on writing certain parts of an SCP article, such as interviews. Examples of such threads include:

  • http://scp-wiki.wikidot.com/forum/t-13834538/dialogue-and-interviews
  • http://scp-wiki.wikidot.com/forum/t-13787438/references-for-ideas-on-interactions-between-foundation-and
  • http://scp-wiki.wikidot.com/forum/t-13696555/containment-procedure-required
  • http://scp-wiki.wikidot.com/forum/t-13695935/how-much-is-too-much-detail

Oftentimes a draft isn't interesting to a reviewer because the core concept is boring/unwieldy. If you're going to ask someone to review an entire sandbox draft, ideally you'd have an interesting concept written up and not just a throwaway practice premise that might introduce issues that will distract a reviewer from focusing on the writing separate from the concept.

item.title: The Metempsychosis Monstrosity
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: Yes

Page Type: SCP Article

Elevator Pitch: A giant formless fleshy monstrosity living in the a part of the Bering Sea. While immobile, the creature is sentient, and appears to be in a constant state of distress. When a living human victim is fed to the creature, it will expel the remains of its last victim, and its new victim will take over its body until a new one is fed to it.

Central Narrative: After discovering the creature and its property, the Foundation appoints General Ferguson in charge of containment, who quickly begins cracking down on the anomaly. Soon after, it is found that the SCP can communicate in simple sentences via a special radio frequency, and the foundation discovers that the anomaly is "hungry" and "hurting", and wants more victims so it can be freed. After this, Ferguson cracks down even more, building a massive concrete wall around the anomaly and ordering constant security, with no one to be anywhere near the creature or have any communication. While many researchers do attempt communication otherwise, they are unable to do much else to help it due to Ferguson's strict orders. Eventually, a d class ends up being fed to it, and there is a massive call among the other d class at the station to feed it another victim to save their comrade.

Hook/Attention Grabber: After this, Ferguson becomes even more strict, with anyone who sympathizes with the anomaly ordered to be imprisoned for treason against the Foundation. Eventually, years later, the anomaly finally moves from its position and makes a charge for Ferguson in a devastating containment breach, with Ferguson being consumed by the end. After this, nearby Foundation ships pick up distress signals from a scared and pained Ferguson calling for backup. The ships attempt to help, but after being met by heavy d class resistance at the station, they compromise with them and agree that the foundation is allowed back in the site as long as they don't help Ferguson, deciding that his tyrannical actions got him what he deserved.

Additional Notes: Hope this isn't too similar to anything else!

item.title: Re: Thaumiel Factory Failure (seeking greenlight)
item.content:encoded:
Took a look at the revised version. It's still too contrivedly overpowered for me to take seriously, especially given that the creator individual somehow knows so much about the Foundation without any solid in-universe reasoning to explain their knowledge. The fact that they just happen to have the means to produce anomalies that could be Thaumiel class (how would they know what Thaumiel class is? Why would they assume Foundation personnel would trust their products, let alone pay for them?) and yet their scheme is disturbed by something as mundane as a coal company just makes the entire story seem sloppily set up.

+ show block
– hide block

Material like this:

They found out about the foundation after witnessing them contain an SCP without getting noticed himself (thorough as the foundation might be) and then began to educate himself on how to make anomalies (not yet specified, more research needed).

just makes me as a reader skeptical. It's already a stretch of disbelief for me to believe that the Foundation just happened to not notice this person witnessing a containment incident (and said person just happens to have the factory means to produce anomalies somehow). When you add in the fact that they somehow learned enough about the Foundation to figure out the kind of anomalies that would be considered useful, and also created a program that can "crack open many cybersecurity features (not all) and then infect every possible device that can print", the result is a story that just feels too forced by authorial meddling to read as genuine or believable.

Why do you want to write about a factory that fails to make certain kinds of anomalies? Why Thaumiel-class items, specifically? Why do you want the factory to be the work of one person? Why do you want them to just randomly and conveniently find out a lot of information about the Foundation, thereby making the Foundation look incompetent in terms of information security?

I feel like so far you've set a lot of difficult challenges up for the story, seemingly for no other reason than you just happen to want to write things that way rather than the narrative organically developing to include those details. Most of these details are problematic because they make the story seem too fake or the main character and their creations too overpowered. How open are you to changing these elements to make the story more believable and the main character more of a relatable individual and not an excessively exceptional caricature?
